title: Consensus and Leader Election
summary: How a cluster of machines agrees on one leader and one ordered log despite crashes and partitions, using majority quorums, Raft terms and elections, and services like etcd and ZooKeeper.

questions.prompt: What problem does **consensus** solve in a distributed system, and why do consensus protocols require a **majority** of nodes to agree rather than, say, any two nodes?
questions.hint: Think about what happens if two separate groups could each make a decision. What do any two majorities of the same cluster always have in common?
keyPoints: Consensus = getting nodes to agree on one value (or one ordered log of values) even when some nodes crash and messages are delayed or lost
Properties: agreement (no two nodes decide differently), validity (decided value was proposed), termination (non-crashed nodes eventually decide)
Any two majorities of the same cluster overlap in at least one node, so two conflicting decisions cannot both get a majority
Overlap means a later quorum always contains a node that knows about earlier committed decisions
Without a majority rule a network partition could let both sides decide independently (split brain)

questions.prompt: For cluster sizes 3, 4, 5 and 7, what is the majority quorum and how many node failures can each tolerate while still accepting writes? Why do people almost never run a 4-node or 6-node consensus cluster?
questions.hint: Quorum is `floor(n/2) + 1`. Failures tolerated is `n - quorum`.
keyPoints: n=3: quorum 2, tolerates 1; n=4: quorum 3, tolerates 1
n=5: quorum 3, tolerates 2; n=7: quorum 4, tolerates 3
General rule: 2f + 1 nodes tolerate f failures
An even-sized cluster tolerates no more failures than the odd size below it, but costs an extra machine and needs one more ack per write
Larger clusters also make every write slower, so 3 or 5 is the usual choice
questions.answer:
| n | quorum | failures tolerated |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 2 | 1 |
| 4 | 3 | 1 |
| 5 | 3 | 2 |
| 7 | 4 | 3 |

4 tolerates the same single failure as 3 (and 6 the same 2 as 5), while adding a machine and one more vote to wait for. So odd sizes, usually 3 or 5.

questions.prompt: In Raft, followers use an election timeout picked **randomly** (for example between 150 and 300 ms) instead of a fixed value. Explain what would go wrong with a fixed timeout, and walk through how an election works.
questions.hint: Imagine five followers all noticing the leader is gone at exactly the same millisecond. Who do they vote for?
keyPoints: Follower that hears no heartbeat before its timeout becomes a candidate: increments the term, votes for itself, sends RequestVote to all
Each node votes at most once per term, and only for a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date as its own
A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats
With identical timeouts all followers become candidates at once, each votes for itself, and nobody reaches a majority (split vote), possibly repeatedly
Random timeouts make it likely one node times out first and wins before others start; after a split vote, a new random timeout and a higher term are used

questions.prompt: A 5-node Raft cluster has its leader in term 7 on node A. A network partition splits it into {A, B} and {C, D, E}. Describe what happens on each side, what happens to a client write sent to A during the partition, and what happens when the partition heals.
questions.hint: Which side can form a majority? What does a node do when it sees a message with a higher term?
keyPoints: A still believes it is leader but can only reach 2 of 5 nodes, so it cannot commit new entries; writes sent to A hang or time out
C, D, E stop hearing heartbeats, one times out and wins an election with 3 votes in term 8, and that side keeps accepting and committing writes
The uncommitted entries on A (and B) were never acknowledged as successful to clients
When the partition heals, A sees term 8 > 7 and steps down to follower
A and B have their conflicting uncommitted log entries overwritten by the new leader's log
No committed write is lost and there is never a second leader that can commit: this is the consistent (CP) choice, the minority side is unavailable

questions.prompt:
A Raft leader keeps `matchIndex`: for each node (including itself) the highest log index known to be stored there. Write `commitIndex(matchIndex)` that returns the highest log index stored on a majority of nodes.

```js
commitIndex([10, 9, 7, 4, 2]); // ?
commitIndex([5, 5, 5, 1]);     // ?
```
questions.hint: Sort the values from highest to lowest. If a majority is `m` nodes, which position in the sorted list is guaranteed to be held by at least `m` nodes?
keyPoints: Majority size is Math.floor(n / 2) + 1
Sort matchIndex descending and return the element at position majority - 1
Sorting numbers in JS needs a comparator: sort((a, b) => b - a), not the default string sort
Results: [10,9,7,4,2] gives 7 and [5,5,5,1] gives 5
Real Raft additionally only advances commit by counting replicas for entries from the leader's current term

questions.prompt: You run 4 copies of a service for availability, but a nightly billing job must run on **exactly one** of them. Design the leader election using etcd or ZooKeeper. How do you stop a paused or partitioned old leader (a "zombie") from double-charging customers?
questions.hint: Think about leases with expiry, what the coordination service gives you when leadership changes, and how the database could reject a stale leader's writes.
keyPoints: Use the coordination service rather than custom code: e.g. etcd lease + compare-and-swap on a key like /billing/leader, or ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential znodes (lowest number wins, each watches its predecessor)
Leadership is tied to a lease or session with a TTL; the leader renews it, and if it dies the key disappears and another instance takes over
A process can pause (GC, VM freeze) past its lease and still believe it is leader, so beliefs alone are not safe
Fencing token: a monotonically increasing number per leadership (etcd revision, ZooKeeper zxid, or Raft term) sent with every write; storage rejects tokens lower than the highest seen
Make the job idempotent too (e.g. unique key per customer per billing period) so even a duplicate run cannot double-charge
Run the etcd/ZooKeeper ensemble itself as 3 or 5 nodes across availability zones
